fields.meta_title: Travel Request Form Builder With Approvals | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Build a travel request form that totals the trip estimate and routes it to the right approver before anything is booked. Free to start.
fields.h1: Build a Travel Request Form That Gets Trips Approved First
fields.hero_description: Describe your travel policy and who signs off. Emergent builds the travel request form, totals each trip estimate and routes it for approval before anyone books.
fields.features_heading: What a Signed PDF Never Checks
fields.features_subheading: A paper request collects the trip details and a signature. Each piece below takes on a check that usually happens over email.
fields.feature_1:
Itemized trip estimates

Ask for airfare and lodging on their own lines, with ground transport and fees below them. The form adds every line, and the approver reads one total with the detail behind it.
fields.feature_2:
Approvers picked by trip type

Send in-state trips to a department head and add a second approver for out-of-state or international travel. Each signature is saved on the request with a name and a time.
fields.feature_3:
Budget left, shown to the approver

Connect each request to its department or project budget. Whoever signs sees what has been spent this year and what would remain if the trip goes ahead, before deciding on it.
fields.feature_4:
A lead-time rule on departure dates

Set how many days ahead trips must be requested. Anything filed inside that window asks the traveler for a reason before it submits, then reaches the approver marked late.
fields.feature_5:
Approved trips sent to the booker

Pass each approved request to whoever books travel, as an email or a Slack message carrying the trip dates and approved amount. Booking stays in the tool your team uses today.
fields.feature_6:
Your code, on your servers

Export the full codebase to your GitHub repository whenever IT wants the travel app hosted in-house. Every request in the database moves too, with signatures attached.

fields.usecase_heading: Four Places Trips Need a Yes First
fields.tab_content_1:
Denver approved with $711 still in the budget

Conference season eats most of the travel money in Ridgemont University's history department. Professor Ana Ruiz asks for three nights in Denver: airfare at $412.00, the hotel at $627.00 and registration at $350.00. Her chair sees a $1,389.00 request with $711 of the $6,000 budget left after it, and approves.
fields.tab_content_2:
Out-of-state trips add a second signature

Harbor Falls approves in-state travel at the department level. A building inspector asks for a four-day code training in Phoenix, and the form sees an out-of-state destination and adds a step. After his department head approves, the town administrator, Ellen Ward, gets the $1,240.00 request as a direct message.
fields.tab_content_3:
Six days of notice comes with a reason

Northfield Advisory bills client travel back to the client, and its policy asks for trips 14 days ahead. A consultant files a Chicago kickoff 6 days before departure. The form will not submit until she explains, and her practice lead sees the request marked late, with her reason beside it.
fields.tab_content_4:
A crew hotel bill worked out before anyone books

Elevator installs at Summit Elevator Services take a crew most of a week on site. The crew lead files one request from his phone: three technicians, 4 nights in Toledo, $139 a night. The form prices the 3 rooms at $1,668 for the operations manager. After approval, the office coordinator gets the names and dates to book.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Travel Request Form
fields.howto_description: Settle the policy before you write the prompt. Two questions shape most of the form: which trips need a second approver, and how much notice is enough.
fields.howto_step_1_des: Pull the rules your organization already follows: which trips need approval and how many days of notice travelers owe. If the policy is silent on either point, settle it with finance now. A form can only enforce rules someone has written down.
fields.howto_step_2_des: List who signs each kind of trip. A department head might cover in-state conferences while out-of-state or international travel needs a second name. Name approvers by role, not by person. Routing by role survives the next reorganization without a rebuild.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Decide which costs travelers must estimate. Airfare and lodging per night are the usual core, with ground transport and conference fees below them. Some employers price meals at the GSA per diem rate for the destination. Fixed lines make requests easy to compare.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Put the approver rules and the notice window into one plain-English prompt, along with the estimate lines. Emergent builds the travel request form and the requests table behind it, with routing between approvers. Ask for changes the same way whenever the policy moves.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Tell the app where each department's travel budget lives, whether that is a spreadsheet or your accounting software. Approvers then see the remaining balance on every request instead of emailing finance to ask what is left this year.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Hand approved trips to the booker
fields.howto_step_6_des: Pick who books once a trip is approved, such as an office coordinator, and whether they hear by email or Slack. Keep the request number with the booking. Receipts filed after the trip can then be matched back to the approval.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Before rollout, file a test trip that departs inside your notice window and crosses state lines. Check that it asks for a reason, reaches both approvers in order and lands in the requests table with each signature and its timestamp.

plan.angle: The live top 10 is blank travel request PDFs from a federal court, universities and public agencies, plus template listings on Scribd, SurveySparrow and Plumsail. Each one collects the traveler, destination, dates, an estimate and signature lines, then leaves routing, the budget check and the booking handoff to email. This page treats the travel request form as approval before money is spent: an itemized estimate, the right approver for the kind of trip, the budget left after the trip, a lead-time rule and an approved request handed to whoever books. It also answers what counts as a travel expense and how a travel request differs from a vacation or visitor request. Receipts filed after the trip stay on the reimbursement and expense report siblings.
